section: 2. The Asset Record — C. Retirement, which most registers never build
quote: A register whose Tier 1 is entirely derived needs no data steward — the only staffing model a conglomerate will sustain, since both the configuration-database and data-catalog failures trace to stewardship roles funded once and never re-funded
problem: This is the report's central thesis (auto-derivation defeats decay) and the vault contains direct counter-evidence that the report cites elsewhere but never confronts here. `servicenow-cmdb-best-practices-2026-guide-virima` is written by a CMDB *auto-discovery vendor* — the party with every incentive to claim discovery removes stewardship — and it nonetheless prescribes 'a named data steward, not a team title, to every CI class', remediation SLAs, weekly health checks and quarterly deep audits, and states flatly that 'CMDB data decay is not a risk, it is a certainty' even under high-frequency automated scanning. So the closest precedent for the report's own answer ran the experiment and still needed the steward. The report uses this source for the discovery-source-stamping detail while ignoring the part that contradicts its thesis, which is the definition of a tension resolved by assertion.
evidence: servicenow-cmdb-best-practices-2026-guide-virima (governance non-negotiables list; 'CMDB data decay is not a risk, it is a certainty'; weekly/quarterly audit cadence); cmdb-vs-asset-management-differences-and-why-you-need-both; why-do-data-catalogue-projects-fail
fix: Replace the sentence with a version that takes the hit and narrows the claim. Suggested: "A register whose Tier 1 is entirely derived removes the *data-entry* steward — the role every adjacent register funded once and never re-funded [cmdb-vs-asset-management-differences-and-why-you-need-both], [why-do-data-catalogue-projects-fail]. It does not remove the maintenance function, and the strongest counter-evidence on this point comes from the automated-discovery vendors themselves: high-frequency scanning is prescribed *alongside* a named steward per class, remediation SLAs and quarterly audits, with decay described as 'not a risk, it is a certainty' [servicenow-cmdb-best-practices-2026-guide-virima]. Auto-derivation therefore buys away the entry cost, not the ownership. What survives is a reconciliation queue — orphaned owners, hash mismatches, expired contracts, unclaimed imports — and the design bar is that this queue stays small enough for the platform owner to be the entire staffing model. If it does not, the CMDB outcome is the base rate, not the exception."

section: 6. The Promote Gate — A. The delivery-performance attack, given full force and then answered
quote: Read what was measured: approval by a body **external** to the change, lacking context, expected to reconstruct the reasoning itself.
problem: The rebuttal survives only by suppressing DORA's own enumeration of the penalized pattern. The source reads: 'approval by people external to the team proposing the change: a change advisory board (CAB) **or a senior manager**.' A senior manager is explicitly inside the measured category. The product's approver is a manager (positioning persona 'Toàn', user #2), so the report answers DORA by describing its design as peer review while its design is the second thing DORA names. That omission makes the opposing case appear in a weakened form at exactly the point the report claims to give it full force.
evidence: dora-capabilities-streamlining-change-approval: 'a heavyweight process involving approval by people external to the team proposing the change: a change advisory board (CAB) or a senior manager'; remedy is 'peer review ... captured in the team's development platform'
fix: Rewrite the rebuttal to quote the full enumeration and pay the cost. Suggested: "Read what was measured: approval by people external to the team proposing the change — 'a change advisory board (CAB) or a senior manager' — lacking context and expected to reconstruct the reasoning itself [dora-capabilities-streamlining-change-approval]. The second term is uncomfortable here, because the approver persona is a manager. DORA's prescribed remedy is peer review captured in the delivery platform, so this design escapes the penalty only on a specific condition: the approver must be the accountable owner closest to the prompt, holding context, deciding from evidence assembled in advance. Routing promotion up a management line instead reproduces precisely what was measured, and an approver who has to go and find the evaluation results is a change-advisory board in miniature that earns the penalty in full."

section: 6. The Promote Gate — B. The legal basis, stated correctly (final paragraph, 'So why keep mandatory approval?')
quote: which makes the human the only mechanism capable of the judgment automation cannot supply. The gate is load-bearing precisely because the evaluation is weak
problem: The report's own strongest cited evidence refutes this. Section 5A quotes the same study reporting that human markers on holistic tasks agreed with each other at ρ=0.054 and MAE 6.84 marks — the report uses that figure to argue the *task*, not the model, is the problem. If the task carries almost no rank information for humans either, then the human approver is not a superior quality discriminator; the report cannot use ρ≈0.054 to indict the judge and then silently assume the human is exempt. Leaving this unengaged is the most damaging unforced error in the argument, because a reader who has read the eval section will catch it.
evidence: criterion-referenceability-determines-llm-as-a-judge-validity-across-physics-ass (human–human pairwise rank agreement ρ=0.054; MAE 6.84 marks) — quoted by the draft itself at §5A
fix: Rewrite the clause so the human's role rests on what humans actually add. Suggested: "...and automated judging carries near-zero rank information on exactly the holistic copy this product's users produce. The honest form of that argument is narrower than it first looks: in the same study human markers agreed with each other at ρ=0.054, so the human is not a better *ranker* of holistic quality either — nobody is. What only an accountable human supplies is consequence judgment and ownership of the outcome: whether *this version stops asking for the customer's budget* is acceptable for this brand, this audience and this quarter. That is why the card renders divergence examples in consequence language and never asks for a quality score. The gate is load-bearing not because the human scores better than the model, but because on this task class scoring is the wrong act and someone must own the decision."

section: 1. What the Asset Framing Commits You To — C. The founding premise is plausible, mechanistically supported, and not measured here
quote: so the *external* figures plausibly reflect benign convergence rather than organizational waste, leaving the internal figures as the defensible analogy
problem: The report applies the 72.8%-prompt-collection-corpus caveat to the external figures only, then treats the 30.4% internal figure as clean and builds the a fortiori on it. But a repository whose purpose is aggregating popular prompts contains near-identical variants of the same prompt *by design* — the caveat cuts at the internal figure at least as hard as at the external one. The report's founding premise therefore rests on the one number it did not discount, discounted for a reason that applies to it too. Given that the run's framing requires the 'measured only on public GitHub repos' objection at full strength, this is the exact place it is softened.
evidence: understanding-prompt-management-in-github-repositories-a-call-for-best-practices (corpus composition 72.8% prompt-collection repositories; internal semantic 30.4%, 28/92); comparisons.md Tension 3
fix: Rewrite so the caveat is applied symmetrically and the inference is carried by the affordances argument rather than by the number. Suggested: "...so the external figures plausibly reflect benign convergence rather than organizational waste — and the same caveat cuts at the internal figures, since a repository built to aggregate prompts holds near-identical variants by design. Neither figure is a clean measurement of organizational waste. What survives is not the number but the affordance argument: this population has version control, code review and searchable history and still duplicates internally at 30.4%" — then keep the existing inference paragraph, and make the falsification test in §12 (scan the group's Drive and Sheets, compare) the thing that carries the premise.

section: 12. Where the Framing Breaks — 'One finding cuts the other way'
quote: **No disinterested source argues against centralizing and governing prompts on the merits.**
problem: Two defects at once. (a) It is an audited absence asserted without stating what was searched — the run directives forbid this. (b) It is contradicted by the vault's own feature-store critique, which objects to centralization on the merits, not on mechanism: sharing one central store 'creates a data dependency', 'Both models need to make a change if one of the models wants to change a feature', versioning 'still requires additional coordination between teams', and the recommended lighter default is a git-maintained catalog of *definitions* offering 'loose coupling between teams' where 'each team can upgrade ... at their own pace'. That is a direct argument that the centralized register is the heavyweight option and a distributed definitions catalog is usually enough — a live objection to this product's shape, and a second independent voice on the git side of the §4 tension. The report reduces that source to 'do not over-borrow the registry pattern'. Separately, the report's claim that 'of the four canonical justifications only discoverability and deduplication map onto prompts' misstates the source: its four are preventing repeated development work, preventing repeated computation, fetching features absent from consumer input, and train-serve skew — and it explicitly says 'This blog post will not focus on data lineage nor discoverability.'
evidence: you-still-dont-need-a-feature-store-xebia (four adoption reasons; 'Sharing a data source between two models creates a data dependency'; feature catalog as loosely-coupled alternative; discoverability explicitly out of scope)
fix: Rewrite the paragraph so the exception is named and the absence carries its search basis. Suggested: "One finding cuts the other way, and one cuts back. Across the literature read for this report — configuration-management, data-catalog, feature-store, model-registry and DevOps-governance sources — every negative voice but one critiques a mechanism while treating governance of the artifact as sound in principle. The exception objects on the merits: centralizing into one shared store 'creates a data dependency' that forces cross-team coordination on every change, and the lighter default proposed is a git-maintained catalog of definitions with 'loose coupling between teams' where each team upgrades at its own pace [you-still-dont-need-a-feature-store-xebia]. That objection lands on this design and the answer has to be scope rather than denial: the register centralizes the *record*, while serving copies stay in each product's own runtime (§8), so no product's release is coupled to another's. Where that separation fails, the objection holds." Then correct the four-justifications sentence to the source's actual four, and note that source explicitly declines to cover discoverability.

section: 2. The Asset Record — A. The decay mechanisms / Tier 1 table (`governance_state`)
quote: MLflow's model registry enforced four fixed stages, then deprecated them after "extensive feedback on the inflexibility of model registry stages."
problem: The report extracts one lesson from MLflow (never hand-set a status) and drops the one the source actually names: *inflexibility* of a fixed enumeration. MLflow's replacement removes the enumeration entirely — freeform tags plus arbitrary user-defined aliases. The report then ships a fixed five-value `governance_state` (imported → claimed → governed → deprecated → retired) while listing 'Any hand-set status enumeration' among the fields the schema refuses. That converts the strongest disinterested counter-precedent in the corpus into unqualified support for a design that inherits half its critique. Secondary provenance point: the vault note is an RFC issue labelled 'stale' and 'Closed as not planned', announcing an intent from MLflow 2.9 — the draft asserts the deprecation as completed fact without saying that removal was not verified here.
evidence: rfc-deprecating-model-registry-stages-issue-10336-mlflowmlflow-github ('extensive feedback on the inflexibility of model registry stages'; replacement = tags + aliases; issue state 'Closed as not planned', label 'stale')
fix: Add one qualifying sentence after the existing MLflow transfer rule in §2A, and tighten the `governance_state` table row. Suggested sentence: "The other half of that feedback was inflexibility, not manual setting — the replacement is freeform tags plus arbitrary aliases, i.e. no fixed enumeration at all — so `governance_state` earns its place only under two conditions: nothing routes on it (aliases move traffic; the state is a derived report), and the enumeration extends without a migration. (The RFC thread itself closed as not-planned; the deprecation is attributable to the MLflow 2.9 announcement recorded in it, not to a removal verified here.)" And change the `governance_state` stale-condition cell to read approximately: "Only if a transition can be set by hand, or if any routing decision reads it. Neither is permitted."

section: 7. Cost and Token Economics — C. Showback before chargeback, gate before chart
quote: To the approver it is binding: a delta above a per-asset threshold requires an explicit override captured in the decision object with a reason.
problem: The report's own resolution of the cost tension makes this number unavailable at the moment it is needed. §7A commits to measuring 'cost per successfully completed task over a traffic sample, including retries and multi-turn recovery, attributed to the prompt version' — none of which exists for a version that has not yet served production traffic. So the flagship USP (cost as a promotion gate rather than a retrospective chart) is gated on a quantity the report has just argued cannot be measured pre-release, and the draft never says what the approver actually sees. Left as is, the sharpest available objection — 'your own measurement rule forbids your own gate' — goes unanswered.
evidence: why-shorter-prompts-can-make-coding-agents-worse (17% input-token cut, 67% session-cost rise, i.e. cost is an end-to-end runtime property); source-tensions.json tension 1 resolution; llm-cost-attribution-at-scale-metadata-tagging-team-budgets-and-chargeback-repor (cost computed at span close from live traces)
fix: Insert two sentences before or after the quoted line stating the estimator and its status. Suggested: "One number the approver cannot be shown is the one the previous section committed to: cost per successful task for a version that has not yet served production traffic. The promote-time figure is therefore a modelled estimate — the candidate replayed over a sample of recent real inputs, priced from the versioned table, retries counted — and it is the weaker of the two measures. The binding measurement arrives after promotion, so the cost threshold also arms a post-promotion alert over the first window of live traffic, and the override record names the estimate it relied on so the two can be reconciled later. That is the honest version of 'cost as a gate': a pre-release estimate that blocks, plus a post-release measurement that can trigger rollback."
length_impact: adds (~85 words) — but this is the one place a bare qualifier will not do, since the USP is at stake

quote: And as the group's own products classify under Vietnam's risk regime, with a 60-day notification clock already run and 12- or 18-month compliance clocks running to March and September 2027
problem: The synthesis silently upgrades §6B's carefully hedged position ('may clear Vietnam's medium- or high-risk classification', 'a plausible component') into an assertion of fact, attaches a legal citation, and concludes the approval record 'becomes a compliance artifact those product teams need'. Read alone — which is how a closing section is read — this reinstates the statutory implication that §6B correctly disclaimed, and it is the exact failure mode the reconciliation flagged as binding: 'Do not let EU AI Act citations imply an obligation that does not bind.'

Suggested: "And to the extent the group's own downstream products fall inside Vietnam's risk regime — a classification question for each product, never for this register, which no regime obliges to gate anything — the approval record is already the artifact those product teams would otherwise have to reconstruct after the fact, against clocks that have partly run [update-decree-1422026nd-cp-guiding-the-artificial-intelligence-law-in-vietnam-vi], [vietnam-artificial-intelligence-law-foundation-and-outlook-insight-baker-mckenzi]."

section: 5. Regression Eval — B. Block on contract, render quality as evidence, monitor for drift
quote: Selecting divergent cases is a retrieval task, not a ranking task, and is therefore not subject to the validity collapse that makes scoring dishonest.
problem: This is the load-bearing move that rescues the eval design — it is what lets the report keep a judge in the loop after having demolished judge validity — and it is asserted with no provenance and no source. It is also contestable on the report's own evidence: surfacing the three-to-five *most* divergent cases is a ranking over divergence, and the style-bias result the report itself cites (judges preferring markdown at 73–97% versus humans at 57%) would bias which differences a judge calls large. Under deep-inference rules this is exactly the derived claim that must name what it derives from and what would falsify it.
evidence: criterion-referenceability-determines-llm-as-a-judge-validity-across-physics-ass; judging-the-judges-a-systematic-evaluation-of-bias-mitigation-strategies-in-llm (residual style bias after nine debiasing strategies); 241021819-self-preference-bias-in-llm-as-a-judge (perplexity-tracking familiarity bias)
fix: Replace the sentence with a provenance-disciplined version that also hardens the implementation. Suggested: "Selecting which cases to surface asks only which two outputs differ most, not which is better, so it does not depend on the rank information the essay study shows a judge lacks [criterion-referenceability-determines-llm-as-a-judge-validity-across-physics-ass]. No source tests that substitution — it is a design inference, and it fails if divergence selection inherits the residual style bias documented after nine debiasing strategies [judging-the-judges-a-systematic-evaluation-of-bias-mitigation-strategies-in-llm]. The mitigation is mechanical: rank divergence on embedding distance and contract-relevant deltas first, and use the model only to caption what changed."

section: 6. The Promote Gate — B. The legal basis, stated correctly
quote: Neither regime obliges a pre-release human sign-off on an internal prompt-management layer, and getting this wrong would not survive counsel review.
problem: A confident universal negative about two legal regimes, stated without the coverage limit the pipeline recorded. The reconciliation is explicit: 'Four Vietnam legal sources remain unread; the jurisdictional conclusion rests on two.' Under the run's provenance rule, an audited absence must say what was searched. The claim is very likely right and should stay committed — but a negative legal claim delivered with a counsel-review flourish and no stated search basis is the one paragraph in the report a lawyer would attack first.
evidence: comparisons.md, 'Open gaps the drafters must not paper over' (four Vietnam legal sources unread); comparisons.md correction 3 (Decree provisions partially unverified)

section: 10. Adoption Inside the Organization — B. The friction budget, spent deliberately (final paragraphs)
quote: Unlike a data catalog, a prompt register is not an index of assets held elsewhere; it is the asset of record, and the serving path requires a canonical store [caching-langfuse].
problem: This is how the report wins the destination-versus-discovery tension, and §8A's highest-leverage architectural decision contradicts it: 'the register must not sit in the hot path', versions are pushed down, 'each product keeps reading from the store it already reads from'. Under that architecture the serving canonical store is the vendor's, and the register is a control plane over copies held elsewhere — materially closer to side A of the tension than the sentence admits. As written, the report wins a tension with a premise its own architecture chapter revokes.
evidence: Draft §8A ('the register must not sit in the hot path'); caching-langfuse and guaranteed-availability-langfuse (serving reliability belongs to the runtime store); source-tensions.json tension 3
fix: Rewrite the clause to separate system-of-record from serving path. Suggested: "Unlike a data catalog, a prompt register is not an index pointing at assets someone else owns; it is the system of record for the artifact itself. That is not the same as being the serving store — §8 deliberately keeps it out of the inference path, with approved versions pushed down into each product's runtime — and the distinction is the whole answer to the destination-versus-discovery objection: one record of truth, serving copies wherever the products already read, capture embedded where prompts are actually written [caching-langfuse], [guaranteed-availability-langfuse]."
